subject: Climate & Environment
title: Textile Waste and Fast Fashion
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Textile Waste and Fast Fashion.

hook.text: The fashion industry produces 92 million tons of textile waste per year. Most is burned or buried.

buildup.text: Fast fashion brands release 52 collections per year — one per week — encouraging constant buying.

discovery.text: The average garment is worn just seven times before being discarded.

twist.text: Synthetic fabrics like polyester shed microplastics with every wash — entering rivers and oceans.

climax.text: Secondhand markets and clothing rental services are growing, but volumes still rise.

punchline.text: Fashion moves fast. The waste it leaves behind doesn't.

quiz.question: How many times is the average fast fashion garment worn?

details.summary: The fashion industry produces over 90 million tonnes of textile waste annually as fast fashion encourages frequent purchases of cheap, disposable clothing. Most discarded garments end up in landfills or are exported to developing countries, where much is burned or dumped rather than reused.
details.whyItMatters: Fast fashion's waste footprint is enormous, yet largely invisible to consumers. Awareness of textile waste is driving demand for slower, more sustainable fashion models.
takeaways: Over 90 million tonnes of textile waste is produced yearly
Fast fashion promotes disposable consumption of clothing
Most discarded textiles end up in landfill or developing nations

faq.question: Where does donated clothing actually go?
faq.answer: Only about 10 to 20 percent of donated clothing is resold locally. The rest is exported to developing countries, where quality has declined as fast fashion saturates donations. Much ends up in open dumps rather than being worn, creating waste problems abroad.

faq.question: How can the fashion industry reduce textile waste?
faq.answer: Strategies include designing for durability, using recyclable mono-materials, implementing take-back programs, investing in fiber-to-fiber recycling technology, and shifting consumer culture toward quality over quantity. Extended producer responsibility legislation can drive systemic change.
